newsitem.title: COSTA RICA: Kissing kidnapper gets 30 years.
newsitem.headline: Kissing kidnapper gets 30 years.

text.p: A former Nicaraguan Contra received a sentence of 30 years in prison late on Friday for his part in the 1996 kidnapping of a German tourist and a Swiss-born tour guide.

Among the evidence presented against Julio Cesar Vega during the trial were photos of Vega kissing the German tourist, Nicole Fleuchaus, as well as love letters and the testimony of her fellow hostage, tour guide Susana Siegried, which pointed to a romance between the abducter and his victim.

Fleuchaus, 25, and Siegfried, 51, were abducted from a nature lodge in northern Costa Rica on New Year's Day 1996 and held in the jungle for 71 days before being released when their families paid $200,000 in ransom.
A three-judge tribunal dismissed defence claims that the photos of Fleuchaus and Vega kissing were evidence of collusion between the two, saying that such behaviour is normal under the circumstances.
"This kind of behaviour is normal given the Stockholm syndrome phenomenon," read the ruling, referring to a tendency for sympathetic bonds to grow between kidnappers and their victims.

Vega received 13 years for the abduction of Fleuchaus and Siegfried, eight years for aggravated robbery of items from the nature lodge, five years for aggravated deprivation of liberty of 25 other people during the abduction, one year for damaging property and three years for illegal possession of arms.
Vega received the sentence impassively, while his mother Maria de Jesus, dissolved into tears at the back of the courtroom.
The tribunal aquitted Vega, 33, and co-defendant Gerbin Garcia, 21, also a Nicaraguan citizen, of a separate 1993 seizure of the Nicaraguan embassy in Costa Rica.
In that case, in which gunmen held 11 people hostage for three weeks, only the group leader, Nicaraguan Contra Jose Urbina Lara, did not wear a mask.
The court found that witness testimony was too weak to firmly establish the identities of three other gunmen wearing masks.
The Contras, aided by covert U.S. backing during the Reagan presidency, fought against the Sandinista government from 1980 until a truce was signed in 1988 and national elections were held in 1990.
